tier_reason: Vendor blog (Tristan Stevens, 2022-10-13) has a summary table with exactly the claimed Kafka vs Redpanda p99.99 numbers (12x/23x/70x). The modified OMB harness is public (redpanda-data/openmessaging-benchmark, linked via PR #37), but the page gives no build/JVM flags or CPU model (only AWS instance types), so this is first-party C, not A.

corrections.caveats: First-party vendor benchmark (Redpanda v22.2.2 vs Kafka v3.2.0, TLS+SASL-SCRAM, 'maximum data safety' configs). Kafka got more nodes than Redpanda in the medium (4 vs 3) and large (6 vs 3) runs. The modified OpenMessaging Benchmark fork is public (github.com/redpanda-data/openmessaging-benchmark; the page links its PR #37), but compiler/JVM flags and CPU models are not stated. Independent rebuttal: Jack Vanlightly (Confluent), 'Kafka vs Redpanda Performance - Do the claims add up?' (2023-05-15), re-ran it with his own OMB fork (github.com/Vanlightly/openmessaging-benchmark-custom) on 3x i3en.6xlarge. He found Kafka misconfigured (log.flush.interval.messages=1 forcing fsync per batch, Java 11), could not get Redpanda to 1000 MB/s with TLS, and saw Redpanda degrade with 50 producers (end-to-end latency up to ~24 s), after ~12 h sustained load (p99.99 ~26 s), with record keys (capped ~330 MB/s vs Kafka 500 MB/s) and at retention limits. He concludes the claims are 'greatly exaggerated'. Treat the 70x as a vendor claim.
corrections.license: BUSL-1.1 (core; converts to Apache-2.0 four years after each release) + Redpanda Community License (enterprise features); GitHub reports no SPDX id
corrections.hardware: AWS: 4x m5n.8xlarge clients (128GB RAM, 32 vCPU, 25Gbps); brokers: i3en.large / is4gen.medium (small, 50MB/s), i3en.3xlarge (medium, 500MB/s), i3en.6xlarge (large, 1GB/s); 3 Redpanda nodes in all tiers vs 3/4/6 Kafka nodes; CPU model not stated

notes: The numbers match the page exactly, and the metadata checks out (12,573 stars, last commit 2026-08-20, not archived, not a fork). The Confluent/Vanlightly 2023 independent re-run disputes the claim and is recorded in caveats; the tier stays C.

tier_reason: The README (benchmark_url) only says 'could be 50 times faster than RabbitMQ'. The detailed page it links (udaparts.com, domain no longer resolves) survives in the Wayback Machine with ms tables and CPU/OS for both machines, and the bench code is in-repo (samples/qperf). Compiler/flags are unstated, it is first-party, and the Kafka comparison has no numbers, so C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Persistent-queue de-queue of 100,000 200-char messages cross-machine: RabbitMQ 44400 ms vs SocketPro 820 ms (~54x, derived from page data; page says 'could be 50 times faster'); en-queue 6873 -> 631 ms (~11x, derived). Page says typically ~8x on de-queue and 8-10x on en-queue. Kafka: 'significantly faster' per README, no numbers.
corrections.hardware: Same-machine test: Acer AT3-605-UR22, Intel Core i7-4770 @3.40GHz, 16GB, Windows 8.1 Pro x64. Cross-machine: client Intel Core i7-3770 @3.40GHz 16GB (Windows 7 Pro x64); broker Intel Xeon E5-2630 v2 @2.60GHz, 4GB, Windows Server 2012R2 in VMware; 1 Gbps per figure (text says 100 Mbps)
corrections.workload: Persistent message queue with auto-ack at the broker: en-queue and de-queue 100,000 messages of 200, 1024 and 10240 chars, same-machine and cross-machine. The RabbitMQ side uses modified rabbitmq-tutorials dotnet NewTask/Worker samples. Driver code is in-repo under samples/qperf (cperf, jperf, rabbitmq/Program.cs, server_queue, kafka_perf_test.txt); no Kafka results published
corrections.caveats: First-party vendor page. The live evidence page (udaparts.com) no longer resolves; numbers are recovered from a 2020 Wayback snapshot (figures are images). Compiler/flags and RabbitMQ version are not stated. The broker ran in a 4GB VMware VM, and the network bandwidth is inconsistent (text 100 Mbps vs figure 1 Gbps). RabbitMQ is not a list baseline, and the Kafka claim has no numbers. There is no LICENSE file: the README calls the plugins 'free', and the core runtime ships as prebuilt binaries (bin/), with only adapters/plugins as source.

notes: The primary evidence page is dead, but the archived copy is traceable and contains the ~50x figure, so I kept the entry at C and pointed benchmark_url at the archive. The metadata matches: 28 stars, last commit 2023-02-16, abandoned, no license, reference.

tier_reason: The README Performance section gives exactly the claimed RTTs vs ZeroMQ, plus the CPU (Xeon E5-2687W), and TCPSHM's own bench is public (test/echo_client.cc, echo_server.cc; test/build.sh: g++ -std=c++11 -O3). The ZeroMQ side's benchmark code, ZeroMQ version and g++ version are not published, so the baseline run is not reproducible: C, not A.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: g++ -std=c++11 -O3 -lrt -lpthread (test/build.sh; g++ version not stated; ZeroMQ build not given)
corrections.claimed_speedup: TCP mode RTT 8.81837us vs ZeroMQ TCP REQ/REP 42.268us (~4.8x, derived from page data); SHM mode RTT 0.338221us vs ZeroMQ IPC (Unix domain socket) 30.6534us (~90.6x, derived from page data)
corrections.caveats: Same-host loopback echo only (not networked). SHM vs ZeroMQ IPC compares busy-polled shared memory against a Unix domain socket, so the ~90x is not apples-to-apples. ZeroMQ benchmark code and version are not in the repo ('exactly the same benchmark method'). g++ version not stated. Busy-polling, no persistence. Inactive since 2020.
